```text
I've read pages 1-5. Let me now read pages 6-10 and 11-16 (especially the appendix). I need to get a thorough understanding of the paper's methods, experiments, and claims.

From what I've read so far:

**Page 1 (Title + Abstract + Intro)**:
- Title: "How Deep Is Your Data? Estimating Recursive Generation Depth via Statistical Fingerprints"
- Anonymous ACL submission
- Abstract: LLMs train on web text containing their own outputs. They formalize recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, 4 generation depths.


- The key findings show that perplexity tail statistics dominate among 19 candidate features, with just the top 5 achieving 97.6% of the full model's performance. A Random Forest classifier reaches 70.3% accuracy on the four-class task (well above the 25% baseline), though performance drops to 58-82.6% when excluding same-strategy comparisons. The zero-shot LLM baseline performs much worse at 36.29%, relying mainly on 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance. Cross-model transfer achieves 66.8% accuracy and cross-strategy transfer reaches 59.1% for extended chains, while testing on C4 web crawl data shows false positive rates between 4.7% and 22.4%.

Now I'm looking at the related work and methodological framing. The field has explored model collapse theory and various AI text detection approaches like DetectGPT and Binoculars, but those focus on binary classification. This work takes a different angle by framing the problem as ordinal classification—estimating how many recursive generation steps produced a given text, where depth 0 is human text and each subsequent depth represents one more round of model finetuning and sampling. The benchmark tests across three model families including Pythia-1.4B and OLMo, treating this as a structured prediction task where the natural ordering between depths matters.

For the generation pipeline, they're using LoRA finetuning with specific hyperparameters to create the recursive training chain, starting from Wikipedia and generating 5000 passages per cycle. The feature engineering extracts 19 statistical measures—perplexity-based, surprisal-based, lexical diversity, and n-gram repetition patterns—though multicollinearity analysis shows most features are highly correlated, suggesting the effective feature space is smaller than the raw count.

Now I'm looking at how they define and measure EDD: for each pair of adjacent depths, they compute a pairwise AUC using a Random Forest classifier on balanced data, then define EDD_T as the maximum depth where all adjacent pairs remain discriminable above a threshold T. The results section shows the four-class accuracy across different model configurations, pairwise AUC decay curves revealing how discriminability drops with depth, and the EDD analysis highlighting where the model loses the ability to distinguish between consecutive generation depths.

I'm seeing that the AUC stays around 0.75 across all three models, and they're examining how well these metrics transfer across different models and strategies.
```
